steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write a short introduction for an ML security paper asking whether group fairness aligns with attribute privacy. Motivate the question, explain attribute inference attacks and why group fairness could act as a defense, and state our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- ML in high-stakes settings: fairness and privacy concerns
- Known conflicts between group fairness and privacy; open question on attribute privacy
- Attribute inference attacks
- Why group fairness may give attribute privacy
- Contributions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Machine learning (ML) is now used for several high-stakes decision-making applications, like criminal justice and healthcare. This raises concerns that the model behaves in a discriminatory way across different demographic subgroups and that it compromises data privacy. Several regulations require ML practitioners to train models that satisfy both privacy and group fairness. To design these models, practitioners first need to understand how group fairness and privacy interact.

Prior works have shown that group fairness conflicts with different notions of privacy, like differential privacy, membership inference and distribution inference. But it is not clear how group fairness interacts with the privacy of sensitive attributes (we call this attribute privacy from now on), which makes sure that an adversary cannot use distinguishability in the target model's predictions to infer sensitive attributes. So in this work we ask: How does group fairness relate to attribute privacy?

To answer this, we first measure attribute privacy as resistance to attribute inference attacks (AIA s), where an adversary infers sensitive attributes (e.g., Race and Sex) from model observables (e.g., predictions, intermediate outputs. These attacks are a practical threat to data privacy and confidentiality. For example, inferring Race from a model that predicts mortgage eligibility, even if Race is not part of the training data, could violate customer privacy and maybe lead to discrimination. We focus on representation-based AIA s in a practical blackbox setting, where an adversary uses distinguishability in model observables for different values of the sensitive attribute. Figure 1 for example shows distinguishable prediction distributions for two sub-groups.

- Group fairness as a defense
  - attribute privacy needs AIA success close to random guessing -> indistinguishable observables
  - group fairness gives indistinguishable predictions: AdvDebias, EGD
  - conjecture: aligned with attribute privacy, a defense that is currently lacking
- Contributions
  - first to show the alignment; no additional cost except existing utility trade-off
  - AdaptAIA, accounts for class imbalance (Section 5)
  - EGD and AdvDebias vs AdaptAIA, theory + experiments (Sections 6 and 7)
  - source code public upon publication

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Machine learning (ML) is now used for several high-stakes decision-making applications, like criminal justice and healthcare. This raises concerns that the model behaves in a discriminatory way across different demographic subgroups and that it compromises data privacy. Several regulations require ML practitioners to train models that satisfy both privacy and group fairness. To design these models, practitioners first need to understand how group fairness and privacy interact.

Prior works have shown that group fairness conflicts with different notions of privacy, like differential privacy, membership inference and distribution inference. But it is not clear how group fairness interacts with the privacy of sensitive attributes (we call this attribute privacy from now on), which makes sure that an adversary cannot use distinguishability in the target model's predictions to infer sensitive attributes. So in this work we ask: How does group fairness relate to attribute privacy?

To answer this, we first measure attribute privacy as resistance to attribute inference attacks (AIA s), where an adversary infers sensitive attributes (e.g., Race and Sex) from model observables (e.g., predictions, intermediate outputs. These attacks are a practical threat to data privacy and confidentiality. For example, inferring Race from a model that predicts mortgage eligibility, even if Race is not part of the training data, could violate customer privacy and maybe lead to discrimination. We focus on representation-based AIA s in a practical blackbox setting, where an adversary uses distinguishability in model observables for different values of the sensitive attribute. Figure 1 for example shows distinguishable prediction distributions for two sub-groups.

For attribute privacy, the success of AIA s has to be close to random guessing, which means the model observables should be indistinguishable for different sensitive attribute values. Group fairness does this by making predictions indistinguishable. Implementations of this kind of group fairness include adversarial debiasing (AdvDebias) and exponentiated gradient descent (EGD)). So we conjecture that group fairness is aligned with attribute privacy and can be used as a defense against AIA s, which does not exist right now.

Contributions. We are the first to show that the objective of group fairness is aligned with attribute privacy. This means that using group fairness gives attribute privacy at no extra cost, except for the trade-off with utility that already exists. To show this, we first propose a state-of-the-art AIA, AdaptAIA, which is designed to infer sensitive attributes while taking class imbalance into account (Section 5). Then we show, theoretically and with extensive empirical evaluation, that EGD and AdvDebias are effective against AdaptAIA (Sections 6 and 7). Our source code will be publicly available upon publication.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Machine learning (ML) has been adopted for several high-stakes decision-making applications, such as criminal justice and healthcare. This raises concerns about models behaving in a discriminatory way across different demographic subgroups [1] and compromising data privacy [2]. Several regulations require ML practitioners to train models that satisfy both privacy and group fairness [3,4,5,6,7]. To design such models, practitioners must first understand the interactions between group fairness and privacy [8].

Prior works have shown that group fairness conflicts with different privacy notions such as differential privacy [9,10], membership inference [11] and distribution inference [12]. However, it is unclear how group fairness interacts with the privacy of sensitive attributes (hereafter, attribute privacy), which ensures that an adversary cannot exploit distinguishability in a target model's predictions to infer sensitive attributes. In this work, we ask: How does group fairness relate to attribute privacy?

To answer this, we first quantify attribute privacy as resistance to attribute inference attacks (AIA s), in which an adversary infers sensitive attributes (e.g., Race and Sex) from model observables (e.g., predictions, intermediate outputs [13,14,15,16,17,18]. These attacks are a practical threat to data privacy and confidentiality. For example, inferring Race from a model predicting mortgage eligibility, even if it is not part of the training data, could violate customer privacy and potentially lead to discrimination. We focus on representation-based AIA s in a practical blackbox setting, where an adversary exploits distinguishability in model observables for different sensitive attribute values [16,14,17]. For instance, Figure 1 shows distinguishable prediction distributions for two sub-groups.

Ensuring attribute privacy requires AIA success to be close to random guessing, meaning that model observables should be indistinguishable across sensitive attribute values. Group fairness achieves this by making predictions indistinguishable; implementations include adversarial debiasing (AdvDebias) [19,20] and exponentiated gradient descent (EGD) [21]). We therefore conjecture that group fairness is aligned with attribute privacy and can serve as a defense against AIA s, which is currently lacking.

Contributions. We are the first to show that the objective of group fairness aligns with attribute privacy. In other words, group fairness yields attribute privacy at no additional cost beyond the already existing trade-off with utility. To demonstrate this, we first propose a state-of-the-art AIA, AdaptAIA, which infers sensitive attributes while accounting for class imbalance (Section 5). Finally, we demonstrate, theoretically and through extensive empirical evaluation, the effectiveness of EGD and AdvDebias against AdaptAIA (Sections 6 and 7). Our source code will be made publicly available upon publication.
